consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same core: the remnant symbolizes the small, faithful minority of God's covenant people whom He graciously preserves through judgment, exile, or apostasy, ensuring the continuity of His redemptive purposes; Paul applies this in Romans 9-11 to the believing minority 'chosen by grace.' Alternatives concern application (dispensationalist future Jewish remnant, Adventist end-time church, mere historical survivors, elect within the visible church), not the core identification.
book_summary: The book defines the remnant as 'the faithful few preserved and gathered from what remains,' using two images: gleanings left at the field's edge (Ruth 2) and gold/silver refined from dross (Zech 13:8-9), anchored also by 1 Kings 19:18 (the 7,000) and Romans 11:5 (remnant according to the election of grace).
consensus_core_identification: The faithful minority of God's people divinely preserved through judgment or apostasy, through whom God's covenant purposes continue.
book_core_identification: The faithful few whom God preserves and gathers from what remains of His people.
boundary_disagreement: None of substance. The book adds the gleaning imagery of Ruth 2, which the consensus responses do not cite, but this is an illustrative metaphor (gathering what is left after the harvest) rather than a change in referent or extension. The refining image from Zechariah 13:8-9 is explicitly present in consensus responses A and B.
material_contradiction: None. Both identify the same referent in the same sense: a divinely preserved faithful minority.
rationale: The book's one-line definition—'the faithful few preserved and gathered from what remains'—is essentially a paraphrase of the consensus core stated by all four responses. Its proof texts overlap directly with the consensus base (1 Kgs 19:18 appears in A and C; Zech 13:8-9 in A and B; Rom 11:5 in all four). The additional 'gathered' emphasis and the gleaning/refining imagery add color but do not narrow, broaden, or reclassify any cases. There is no boundary dispute, no denial of any consensus application, and no novel referent.
strongest_objection: One could argue the Ruth 2 citation introduces a slightly novel angle—the remnant as gleanings gathered by a redeemer figure—since Ruth 2 is not a standard remnant proof text and Ruth herself is a Moabite outsider rather than a preserved Israelite minority; if the chapter builds heavily on that, the book might subtly broaden the remnant to include gathered outsiders. But on the entry alone this is metaphorical illustration, not a redefinition.
